subtype: Approach: help neighbours through community coordination [Action]
passage:
Madhav: After you reached the school shelter, what did you do?

Maria: Honestly? Sat on a mat for one night. Then I saw a notice: the local volunteer group needed hands. I signed up, and the ward officer gave us a list of elders living alone. We didn't wade anywhere. The officer told us which lanes were safe, and the boats went to the others. My job was carrying dal and rice packets and knocking on doors with a checklist. We ticked each name, noted who needed the health volunteer to visit, and handed the sheet back to the officer at the end of the day. At first I wanted to run to the worst lane myself. I was impatient and wanted to do something big. It turned out to be better that we worked as a group, and every name got a visit.

qa.q: What did the ward officer give the volunteers?
qa.a: The ward officer gave the volunteers a list of elders living alone.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when wanting to run to the worst lane?
qa.a: Maria felt impatient and eager to do something big, but accepted the group plan.

qa.q: What could go wrong if volunteers each went alone, and what works better?
qa.a: Lone volunteers could end up in unsafe lanes and miss people, while working with the officer covers more homes safely.

qa.q: How might an elder living alone see the volunteers' visit?
qa.a: The elder would probably feel relieved and cared for, being checked on by someone with a list and food rather than being forgotten.

grounding: Illustrates a student joining a volunteer group and working with authorities to deliver food and check on elders after reaching safety.

passage:
I'm Tarun, and I live two doors down from Divyansh in the relief camp at the district school. After the floods, when we'd all got here safely, I expected him to go back and try rescuing people himself. He's that kind.
Instead, on the second morning, he walked over to the volunteer desk set up by the municipal officials and signed a register. They gave him an armband and a list: twelve houses on higher ground where old people were still living alone.
For four days I watched him leave each morning with two other volunteers and a sack of food packets from the government store. They went by the route the officials had marked. Each evening he gave his list back with notes: who needed medicines, who wanted to come to the camp.
On the fifth day an old woman from one of those houses arrived at the camp, holding his arm. I can't say what he felt, but he looked very tired and very steady.

qa.q: How many houses were on Divyansh's volunteer list?
qa.a: There were twelve houses on higher ground where old people lived alone.

qa.q: What might Divyansh have been feeling when he chose the volunteer desk instead of rescuing alone?
qa.a: He may have felt a strong urge to help mixed with caution, choosing the organised route over a risky solo effort.

qa.q: Why was working through the volunteer desk wiser than going out alone?
qa.a: The officials knew the safe routes and which houses needed help, so Divyansh could help more people without becoming someone who needed rescuing.

qa.q: How might the old woman who came to the camp feel about Divyansh's visits?
qa.a: She would likely feel grateful and safe, trusting him enough to hold his arm on the way to the camp.

grounding: Shows the student, once safe, joining a volunteer group run with officials to deliver food and check on elders instead of acting alone.

passage:
Day one after the water came down. Nirmala and her family were safe at her aunt's house on the hill. From the window she saw young men wading into the flooded lanes alone, shouting names. She wanted to go too.
Day two. Her friend Bhavna phoned. "The ward office has started a volunteer group with the disaster response team. They need people who know the lanes." Nirmala went that afternoon. An officer took her name, gave her a vest, and put her with four others. Their job: check on elderly residents in Block C and report who needed food or a doctor.
Day four. Nirmala had knocked on thirty doors. Two old men had been without food for a day; the team brought packets from the ward store and radioed for a doctor for one of them. When a lane was too deep, the team leader said no, and they went round. Nirmala was exhausted, but she hadn't taken a single risk alone.

qa.q: How many doors had Nirmala knocked on by day four?
qa.a: Nirmala had knocked on thirty doors.

qa.q: What did Nirmala feel when she saw young men wading into the lanes alone?
qa.a: She felt a strong urge to help and wanted to go too, even though it would have been risky.

qa.q: Why was the team approach better than wading in alone?
qa.a: The team knew which houses to check, had supplies and a doctor to call, and a leader who turned back when a lane was too deep.

qa.q: How might the two old men without food have felt when the team arrived?
qa.a: They likely felt relieved and less alone after a day without food, especially when a doctor was called for one of them.

grounding: Shows a student, after reaching safety, joining a volunteer group working with the authorities to deliver food and check on elders safely.
